scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Songpasandae-nori took shape in the 19th century in the Songpa Market, then a preeminent commercial trading center in the Gyeonggi province.
It preserves the classic Joseon Dynasty form of sandae-nori.
After the severe Han River flood of 1925 submerged and ruined Songpa Village, surviving residents relocated nearby to Garak-dong and Seokchon-dong, continuing the theatrical tradition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically staged during major seasonal holidays including Jeongwol daeboreum (First Full Moon), Dano (Spring festival), Baekjung (All Souls Day / mid-autumn festival), and Chuseok (Harvest festival), as well as occasional royal court command performances.
During Baekjung festivities, celebrated players gathered to perform for an entire week.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear dramatic theatrical costumes and specialized wooden or papier-mâché masks throughout the parade and play.
There are thirty-three masks in total, notable for incorporating character types such as the dangnyeo, Haesaneomeom, Sinhalmeom, and mudang (shaman).
The traditional staging ground was the open-air Songpa Market; today, it is primarily preserved and taught at the outdoor Seoul Nori Madang performance amphitheater near Seokchon Lake.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Songpasandae-nori is the regional metropolitan variant preserved from Songpa, Seoul.

A branch of sandae-nori developed in Seoul and the central metropolitan region during the Joseon Dynasty, maintained by merchant community lineages in Garak-dong and Seokchon-dong following the 1925 Han River flood.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Songpasandaenori is sibling of Yangju byeolsandae nori: Both are sandae-nori mask dramas from the Seoul and Gyeonggi capital region, distinguished by specific mask sets.
Songpasandaenori is parent of Talchum: Songpasandae-nori is an urban tradition within the broader Korean talchum mask drama family.
Songpasandaenori is sibling of Namsadang nori: A related itinerant Korean folk performance tradition sharing festive market settings.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Includes seomakgosa, an opening jesa sacrificial rite offering food, poured liquor, and prostrations to honor the dead, accompanied by protective amulets to ward off misfortune.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: At the edge of Seoul's Seokchon Lake, performers don 33 grotesque masks to invoke ancestral spirits, parody corrupt elites, and revive the resilient theatre of old Songpa Market.
